deals.body: Buy 3 Get 1 Free Halal cheese tart counter Hokkaido Baked Cheese Tart is running a Buy 3 Get 1 Free on its cheese tarts for 11.11, from Saturday 7 to Wednesday 11 November 2026. Unlike its September anniversary 1-for-1, which split two outlets per day and covered the Original only, this one runs across the whole range, so flavoured tarts count too. The catch is in the brand's own caption: the free tart has to be of lower or equal value to the ones you pay for, and it is while stocks last. The chain is now down to three Singapore outlets after Bugis Junction closed on 10 September: Jurong Point, Parkway Parade and Changi Airport Terminal 3.

deals.body: 1-for-1, $2++ plates Sushi Express and Sushi Plus are running a 1-for-1 on one featured sushi plate a day, from 1 to 23 November 2026, at all 21 Sushi Express and 3 Sushi Plus outlets. The plate changes with the day of the week: Caramelised Salmon on Mondays, Cheesy Thick Cut Unagi on Tuesdays, Mentai Salmon on Wednesdays, Hanamaki on Thursdays, Mentai Salmon Belly Inari on Fridays, Eel & Tamagoyaki on Saturdays and Tuna Salmon Donburi on Sundays. The poster prints all featured plates at $2++, which is about $2.40 nett after service charge and GST. There are 16 days left from Sun 8 Nov, and the last day, Mon 23 Nov, is a Caramelised Salmon day. T&Cs apply and it is while stocks last. The brand's 争鲜gogo takeaway kiosks are not named in the post.

deals.body: Up to 70% off NITORI Singapore is running a Furniture Outlet Sale of B-Grade furniture at up to 70% off, from Friday 6 to Sunday 22 November 2026, and only at its Bugis Junction store (#03-11, open daily 10am to 10pm). The official posters name three categories: electric recliner sofas, dining tables and chairs, and office chairs, plus 'many more clearance items'. The 70% is a ceiling on selected products, not a storewide cut, and B-Grade means display or lightly imperfect pieces sold while stocks last, so each item is a one-off. NITORI has not published item prices, so check each tag in store, inspect the piece, and ask about delivery and returns before paying.

members.body:
KFC is collaborating with Marvel for a new Doomsday menu
Image credit: KFC
Marvel’s movies have been a pivotal part of my life growing up. I remember being wholly captivated by the flashy images of laser beams and explosions while chowing down on buckets of fried chicken . Now, two different parts of my childhood have collided: KFC Singapore and Marvel Studios are working together to launch a new collaboration menu on 25 November 2026 , inspired by Avengers: Doomsday and its latest villain, Doctor Doom.
KFC’s Samyang Buldak Carbonara Is Back With New Macaroni Bowl For A Limited Time
Image credit: KFC
The most notable menu item is the Doom Burger (price TBD) , which puts an “evil” twist on KFC’s signature Zinger burger that’s fit for an apocalyptic villain like Doctor Doom. It comprises two black, charcoal-infused hamburger buns sandwiching a crispy chicken fillet that’s dressed in a strikingly green chipotle-lime seasoning for a tangy bite. It is then topped with lettuce and sliced cheese, then finished with their unique collab sauces: jalapeno ranch and cola sauce.
Image credit: KFC
Alternatively, order their Doom Chicken (price TBD) , featuring KFC’s iconic crispy fried chicken coated in the same zingy chipotle-lime seasoning that’s said to cut through the richness. It’s accompanied by the aforementioned jalapeno ranch and cola sauce for a bite that hits all flavour notes at once.
Image credit: KFC
If you’re itching for a snack instead, the Doom Chicken Bites (price TBD) may be up your alley. It’s the same crispy chicken and chipotle-lime seasoning combo but scaled down to dippable, bite-sized pieces, served with the same two sauces.
Image credit: KFC
For some satisfying cheese pulls, get the Masked Mozza Melts (price TBD) : stretchy mozzarella cheese coated in a crunchy batter. You can even sauce things up with a complimentary dip.
Image credit: KFC
Wash it all down with their Doom Fizz (price TBD) , a refreshing drink made of soda water zhnged up with green apple and kiwi syrup. It’s said to be sweet and fizzy—the perfect sidekick to battle the heat.
Image credit: KFC
That’s not all: for every purchase of any Doctor Doom menu item, you’ll get an exclusive Colonel Sanders Cosplay Collection Figurine , featuring the iconic KFC mascot, Colonel Sanders, decked out in Marvel character-inspired looks. There are five different character designs, namely Cyclops , Doctor Doom , Gambit , The Thing , and Thor . As a die-hard X-Men fan, my favourite has to be Cyclops.
If you’re counting down to the film’s cinema debut, this is a solid excuse to make a KFC run. The menu’s release date isn’t out yet, though, so stay tuned for further updates.
Another iconic chain collaboration is Starbucks x Pompompurin , which launches a few Singapore-exclusive merch items and more from 10 November 2026. Additionally, check out our guide to the best food deals in November 2026 for collaborations such as Opus Bar & Grill x Old Chang Kee, lobangs and more.
Website | Full list of outlets
KFC is halal-certified.

The Orchard Cafe at Orchard Hotel Singapore is running its Christmas buffet from 2 November 2026 to 3 January 2027, with Christmas Day lunch at S$138++ and dinner at S$150++. Ordinary weekday lunches start at S$94++, and bookings made by 10 December take 30 per cent off.
The spread goes by the name Made for Merry Gatherings this year. Its centrepieces include a whole turkey roasted with French-style butter and black truffle, and Himalayan salt-baked salmon.
Prices from now to 3 January
• Monday to Thursday: lunch S$94++, dinner S$108++
• Friday and Saturday lunch: S$104++
• Friday to Sunday dinner: S$118++
• Sunday brunch: S$128++
On ordinary days, lunch runs from 12pm to 2pm and dinner from 6pm to 9.30pm. All prices are in Singapore dollars and carry service charge and GST on top.
Festive buffet prices before service charge and GST. Image: Orchard Hotel Singapore
Christmas and New Year dates
Christmas Eve falls on a Thursday this year. Lunch is S$120++ and dinner S$150++, served in two seatings, 5.30pm to 7.30pm and 8pm to 10pm.
Christmas Day lunch is S$138++, with seatings from 11.30am to 1pm and from 1.30pm to 3pm. Dinner is S$150++ over the same two evening seatings as the night before.
On New Year’s Eve, lunch is S$120++. Dinner costs S$148++ for the 5.30pm to 7.30pm seating and S$168++ for the later one, from 8pm to 10pm.
New Year’s Day lunch is S$104++ and dinner S$118++.
What is on the buffet
Salads open with roasted pear and fig on orange quinoa with feta, and a Nyonya-style turkey kerabu. The charcoal grill turns out tiger prawn kebabs, grilled beef ribs and Spanish-style barbecue pork belly. Elsewhere there is wagyu beef cottage pie, duck leg confit, baked oysters and pork rib in champagne sauce, plus a hot-plate wagyu beef burger and a creamy peanut miso ramen with turkey.
Christmas and New Year’s Eve dinners add pass-around canapés from chef Thenesh: grilled wagyu beef, duck confit and butternut arancini, Hokkaido scallop crudo and durian spring rolls. Christmas diners also get a signature wagyu beef pastrami panini.
Desserts stay traditional. Expect minced fruit pie, marzipan stollen, mixed fruit cake, berry sherry trifle, panettone pudding and cinnamon star cookies, with lychee champagne ice jelly for something cold.
The Orchard Cafe at Orchard Hotel Singapore. Image: Orchard Hotel Singapore
Discounts for members, seniors and children
The early-bird rate is 30 per cent off for bookings made by 10 December 2026 and 25 per cent off for bookings from 11 December.
MyMillennium members eat 1-for-1 for the first 50 diners, and members after that get 30 per cent off. Seniors aged 65 and above pay half price at lunch and dinner. Children below six eat free, and children aged six to 12 pay half the adult price.
These offers cannot be combined. Whether early-bird and member rates cover Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year’s Eve or New Year’s Day is not stated, so ask when you reserve.
Booking a table
Reservations are required. The Orchard Cafe is at Orchard Hotel Singapore, 442 Orchard Road, and takes bookings on 6739 6565 or through its TableCheck reservations . The menu rotates and can change without notice.

Dim sum buffets in Singapore
If you’re like me and would die happy with all the dim sum you could eat, Singapore offers plenty of dim sum buffets starting at just $ 1 6.80++ that are perfect for any occasion. Here’s a complete guide to affordable dim sum buffets in Singapore.
1. TungLok Teahouse
Image credit: @blurfoodie
TungLok Teahouse is a popular dim sum buffet option in Singapore among families, with its interior designed to create a convivial atmosphere to sip and chat over a good cup of tea. The A La Carte Dinner Buffet is priced at $26.80++ per person from Monday to Thursday, and $29.80++ from Friday to Sundays. There’s also the High Tea Buffet , priced at $16.80++ per person on weekdays and $21.80++ per person on weekends.
What’s better is that they are one of the few options for unlimited dim sum during dinnertime, which puts them head and shoulders above those catering to just the lunch and teatime crowd. Do note that a minimum of two people are needed to book a table for the buffet. Outside of dim sum, diners are entitled to Chinese delicacies such as their Chilli Prawn with Fried ‘Mantou’ on weekdays, Sweet and Sour Pork Chop on weekends and more.
Read our Tunglok Teahouse feature .
Address: 10 Sinaran Drive, #01-73, Square 2, Singapore 307506
Buffet hours: Daily 3pm to 5pm (High Tea Buffet), Daily 6pm to 10pm (A La Carte Dinner Buffet)
Tel: 6893 1123
Website
TungLok Teahouse is not halal-certified.
TungLok Teahouse Has $16.80++ Dim Sum High Tea Buffet In Novena
2. Swatow Seafood
Image credit: Swatow Seafood
One might think seafood is the speciality of Swatow Seafood , but they are more commonly known for dishing out affordable dim sum. Drop by their Toa Payoh outlet for their High Tea Dim Sum Buffet that’s available daily at $ 33.80 ++ on weekdays and $38.80++ on weekends, with over 20 types of handcrafted dim sum selections, including crab and prawn dishes, and even a sweet treat to end your meal!
Address: 181 Lorong 4 Toa Payoh, #02-602, Toa Payoh Hub, Singapore 310181
Buffet hours: Daily 3pm to 5pm
Tel: 6363 1717
Website
Swatow Seafood is not halal-certified.
3. Yum Cha Restaurant
Located in Chinatown and Changi , Yum Cha Restaurant offers traditional Cantonese dim sum. Decked in marble tables and wooden chairs, Yum Cha brings back the nostalgia of a traditional dim sum teahouse. Order your favourite bite-sized dim sum buffet delicacies at their Changi outlet during their Weekday Dinner Buffet at $36.80++ per person . Popular picks include the Yum Cha Prawn Dumpling , Baked Mini Egg Tarts and Peking Duck Roll . If dim sum is not your thing, they offer other dishes such as Seafood Fried Rice , Stir Fry Ee Fu Noodle with Mushroom and more.
Read our Yum Cha review .
Changi outlet
Address: 6 Changi Business Park Avenue 1, #01-33, UE BizHub East, Singapore 486017
Buffet hours: Mon -Fri 5:30pm to 9p m
Tel: 6789 1717
Websit e
Yum Cha is not halal-certified.
Yum Cha Review: Dim Sum Buffet With Over 60 Items For $32.80++ At Chinatown
4. Ban Heng
As much as gorging on 20 dim sum items during an All – You – Can – Eat Ala-Carte Buffet sounds like a good plan, Ban Heng charges extra for food wastage, so order only what you can stomach! Prices start at $39.80++ per person on weekdays and $45.80++ per person on weekends at both their Orchid Country Club and Boon Keng outlet s.
Expect a wide range of dim sum items such as Charco a l Musang King “Liu Sha” Bun , Deep-Fried Banana & Red Bean Roll , and Steamed Crystal Chive Dumpling Shrimp . Better yet, one diner gets to eat for free with every three paying adults.
Boon Keng outlet
Address: 22 Boon Keng Road, #01-21, Singapore 330022
Buffet hours: Thurs-Tue 11:30am to 3pm, 6pm to 10:30pm
Tel: 6291 0407
Orchid Country Club outlet
Address: 1 Orchid Club Road, #02-35, Social Club House, Orchid Country Club, Singapore 769162
Buffet hours: Daily 11:30am to 3pm, 6pm to 10pm
Tel: 6732 7888
Website
Ban Heng is not halal-certified.
5. Hai Tien Lo
Image credit: @haitienlo
Located at Pan Pacific Singapore , Hai Tien Lo offers a Cantonese dim sum brunch buffet . Priced at $ 72 ++ per person on weekdays and $ 82 ++ on weekends, Hai Tien Lo boasts a myriad of luxurious eats from Steamed Charcoal Barbecue Pork Bun with Black Truffles to Deep Fried Kataifi Seafood Roll with Pomelo and Mango . They even offer a special menu that spans over 10 items, including the Stewed Beef Brisket with Tendon and Carrot and a Barbecued Meat Trio Platter .
Address: 7 Raffles Boulevard, Level 3, Pan Pacific Singapore, Singapore 039595
Buffet hours: Daily 11:30am to 2:30pm, 6pm to 10:30pm
Tel: 6826 8240
Website
Hai Tien Lo is not halal-certified.
6. TungLok Seafood
Image credit: @inoutspot

deals.body:
Habibi Kebs has affordable doner kebabs in Kembangan
Doner kebabs are low-key an underrated option for a fast and affordable meal : they’re quick to prepare, portable, and packed full of vegetables for your daily dose of vitamins. So, next time you’re in Kembangan running errands or passing by on your daily jog along the park connectors, check out Habibi Kebs , a Muslim-owned eatery serving Berlin-inspired doner kebabs at nett prices.
Food at Habibi Kebs
For the uninitiated: doner kebabs are a traditional Turkish dish. The word “doner” comes from the Turkish term “dönmek”, meaning to “turn” or “rotate”, which aptly describes how it’s cooked: seasoned meat, usually chicken, beef, or lamb, is stacked on a vertical rotisserie and cooked until crispy on the outside and juicy within.
Habibi Kebs is a no-frills store specialising in authentic doner kebabs. The founders shared with us that they both have had prior culinary experience, and after a hiatus, they both decided to come together to start Habibi Kebs to bring the German doner experience to the masses. Contrary to traditional Turkish doner that’s served with rice, grilled vegetables, or tombik (AKA Turkish round pocket loaf) with little sauces and salads, German doner goes heavy on salad and sauces: all dressed and packed into bread for a portable, street-food-style sandwich.
The menu’s pretty straightforward: choose from three main styles, your protein of chicken, beef, or a mix of both, and a sauce: Garlic Sauce , Chili Sauce , or Herb Sauce . If you want it more saucy, you can top up $1 for an additional sauce.
If you’re feeling peckish, you can even upgrade your meal for an additional $5 , which comes with a side of fries and a soft drink.
We first got their signature Chicken Doner Kebab with Garlic and Chili Sauce ($11) . You get doner bread, AKA Turkish flatbread, stuffed with lettuce, tomatoes, jalapenos, red onions, red cabbage, and chicken, dressed in a spicy chilli and zingy garlic sauce.
The doner bread had a nice crusty exterior and a soft, fluffy interior, making the perfect base for the whole dish. The chicken was well marinated and slightly smoky, which complemented the fresh vegetables.
We also tried their Beef Durum with Garlic and Herb Sauce ($11) , which featured the same medley of lettuce, tomatoes, jalapenos, red onions, red cabbage, and grilled minced beef, drenched in a zingy garlic and herb sauce. The whole shebang was tightly wrapped in durum bread, similar to a burrito you’d get from Stuff’d.
The minced beef was nicely charred and finely minced, while the vegetables helped cut through some of its richness. I particularly liked how the durum was left under a press grill for a while, giving it a crunchy exterior for some textural contrast.
Worth noting: the owner mentioned that the minced beef is likely being phased out soon, so head down sooner rather than later if you want to try this combo.
Last but not least, we ordered the Mixed Doner Teller with Garlic and Herb Sauce ($14) . It featured a bed of golden-brown, thick-cut fries loaded with both aforementioned meats, lettuce, jalapenos, tomatoes, red cabbage, and red onions, then finished with a drizzle of garlic and herb sauces.
Usually, I’m wary of loaded fries as they tend to turn soggy fast. However, the fries here were still crispy on the outside and fluffy on the inside. They were generously loaded with toppings, and I particularly enjoyed how the vegetables and herb sauce helped to mellow out the richness.
We also had the opportunity to try one of their unreleased items: the Quesadilla ($12) , which featured doner chicken, mozzarella, and chili sauce encased in a tortilla wrap, and grilled till crunchy on the outside.
Without a doubt, this was our favourite dish of the bunch: cheesy and creamy, with a little kick from the chili sauce.
The release date is currently TBD, though the owner told us it could be as early as this month. So, do keep a lookout on their Instagram page for any updates.
Finally, we washed it all down with Salaam Cola ($3) , a soft drink hailing from Ireland that was refreshing on a hot day. It was sweet and fizzy, and tasted similar to Coke. The brand that produces Salaam Cola also donates 10% of their profits to conflict-afflicted regions.
Ambience at Habibi Kebs
The eatery is decked out in a vibrant red-and-white aesthetic reminiscent of an American diner. If you’re dining in, there are also a few chairs outside so you can sit down and enjoy your meal. You’ll definitely need it, as the interior of the store itself is squeezy with little ventilation, which isn’t an ideal condition for you to enjoy a sandwich in.
When we visited the store on a weekday lunch, there wasn’t much of a crowd, so we didn’t need to wait much for our food to arrive. However, the traffic did start to pick up after we got our food, so do come early if you’d like to skip the queue.
Habibi Kebs is located a five-minute walk from Kembangan MRT Station .

members.body:
Habibi Kebs has affordable doner kebabs in Kembangan
Doner kebabs are low-key an underrated option for a fast and affordable meal : they’re quick to prepare, portable, and packed full of vegetables for your daily dose of vitamins. So, next time you’re in Kembangan running errands or passing by on your daily jog along the park connectors, check out Habibi Kebs , a Muslim-owned eatery serving Berlin-inspired doner kebabs at nett prices.
Food at Habibi Kebs
For the uninitiated: doner kebabs are a traditional Turkish dish. The word “doner” comes from the Turkish term “dönmek”, meaning to “turn” or “rotate”, which aptly describes how it’s cooked: seasoned meat, usually chicken, beef, or lamb, is stacked on a vertical rotisserie and cooked until crispy on the outside and juicy within.
Habibi Kebs is a no-frills store specialising in authentic doner kebabs. The founders shared with us that they both have had prior culinary experience, and after a hiatus, they both decided to come together to start Habibi Kebs to bring the German doner experience to the masses. Contrary to traditional Turkish doner that’s served with rice, grilled vegetables, or tombik (AKA Turkish round pocket loaf) with little sauces and salads, German doner goes heavy on salad and sauces: all dressed and packed into bread for a portable, street-food-style sandwich.
The menu’s pretty straightforward: choose from three main styles, your protein of chicken, beef, or a mix of both, and a sauce: Garlic Sauce , Chili Sauce , or Herb Sauce . If you want it more saucy, you can top up $1 for an additional sauce.
If you’re feeling peckish, you can even upgrade your meal for an additional $5 , which comes with a side of fries and a soft drink.
We first got their signature Chicken Doner Kebab with Garlic and Chili Sauce ($11) . You get doner bread, AKA Turkish flatbread, stuffed with lettuce, tomatoes, jalapenos, red onions, red cabbage, and chicken, dressed in a spicy chilli and zingy garlic sauce.
The doner bread had a nice crusty exterior and a soft, fluffy interior, making the perfect base for the whole dish. The chicken was well marinated and slightly smoky, which complemented the fresh vegetables.
We also tried their Beef Durum with Garlic and Herb Sauce ($11) , which featured the same medley of lettuce, tomatoes, jalapenos, red onions, red cabbage, and grilled minced beef, drenched in a zingy garlic and herb sauce. The whole shebang was tightly wrapped in durum bread, similar to a burrito you’d get from Stuff’d.
The minced beef was nicely charred and finely minced, while the vegetables helped cut through some of its richness. I particularly liked how the durum was left under a press grill for a while, giving it a crunchy exterior for some textural contrast.
Worth noting: the owner mentioned that the minced beef is likely being phased out soon, so head down sooner rather than later if you want to try this combo.
Last but not least, we ordered the Mixed Doner Teller with Garlic and Herb Sauce ($14) . It featured a bed of golden-brown, thick-cut fries loaded with both aforementioned meats, lettuce, jalapenos, tomatoes, red cabbage, and red onions, then finished with a drizzle of garlic and herb sauces.
Usually, I’m wary of loaded fries as they tend to turn soggy fast. However, the fries here were still crispy on the outside and fluffy on the inside. They were generously loaded with toppings, and I particularly enjoyed how the vegetables and herb sauce helped to mellow out the richness.
We also had the opportunity to try one of their unreleased items: the Quesadilla ($12) , which featured doner chicken, mozzarella, and chili sauce encased in a tortilla wrap, and grilled till crunchy on the outside.
Without a doubt, this was our favourite dish of the bunch: cheesy and creamy, with a little kick from the chili sauce.
The release date is currently TBD, though the owner told us it could be as early as this month. So, do keep a lookout on their Instagram page for any updates.
Finally, we washed it all down with Salaam Cola ($3) , a soft drink hailing from Ireland that was refreshing on a hot day. It was sweet and fizzy, and tasted similar to Coke. The brand that produces Salaam Cola also donates 10% of their profits to conflict-afflicted regions.

JJAN is a new Korean tapas bar in Tanjong Pagar
Image credit: JJAN
If your Korean nights out usually stop at green soju bottles and a plate of fried chicken, here’s a new spot that goes further. JJAN , a Korean tapas bar opening on 12 November 2026 along Craig Road in Tanjong Pagar , pours more than 30 types of makgeolli and brews by the glass. The bar is headed by a chef who previously worked at the two-Michelin-starred Saint Pierre.
Tanjong Pagar Food Guide: 20 Places For Michelin-Approved Pizza, Korean Knife-Cut Noodles And More
The name comes from what Koreans say when they clink glasses. The whole concept is built on juansang, the Korean custom of serving food specifically to go with drinks, so the dishes are meant to sit alongside a glass rather than compete with it.
Image credit: JJAN
Executive Chef Yoo Gwangsoo runs the kitchen. Before Saint Pierre, he worked at Jean-Georges in Dubai and at Lab XXIV in Seoul and Busan. At JJAN, he applies French techniques to Korean drinking food and uses some local produce.
Image credit: JJAN
Makgeolli is the main draw here, and the rotating list covers more than the sweet, milky bottles you’d find at the supermarket. Expect light, fresh brews, thicker and stronger takju, naturally sparkling versions, and unpasteurised saeng makgeolli. Saeng makgeolli still has live yeast and spoils quickly, so it needs an unbroken cold chain and rarely makes it to Singapore. Founder Lee Haedong visited breweries across Korea to pick the labels, and many are new to Singapore.
Image credit: JJAN
There are also clear rice liquors, yakju, and cheongju. They look a lot like sake but are fermented with nuruk, a traditional Korean starter, which gives them their own aromas. Top picks to look out for include the golden Midam Seoktanju ($19++) , whose name roughly means “a wine too good to swallow”, and the drier Suamju ($18++) , which has melon and Korean pear notes.
The wine list leans towards bottles from Korean winemakers working in France, including Burgundy’s Lou Dumont.
Image credit: JJAN
Every meal starts with two house-made table snacks: a crisp sesame jeonbyeong cracker and prawn chips dusted with chilli salt.
Among the small bites, the Squid Ganghoe ($6++ per piece) wraps poached squid around six vegetables, including doraji (bellflower root), with citrus and a spicy chogochujang dip. Mushroom fans should look at the Pyogo Jeon ($5++ per piece) , a fried shiitake stuffed with sea bass and prawn mousse and glazed with perilla-leaf soy.
The sharing plates are more involved. The Yukhoe ($34++) is a build-your-own Australian Wagyu tartare with fermented octopus, Korean pear, and crispy seaweed chips. The Busan Jijimi & Squid Salad ($19++) is a mung bean pancake made with local kueh chye (garlic chives), and you wrap the squid salad in it, while the the Deep-Fried Oyster Ssam ($22++) comes with lettuce from Greenphyto, a farm in Jurong West.
Image credit: JJAN
For mains, the Pork Gukbap ($21++) looks like the comfort pick. It’s a pork bone broth simmered for 48 hours and served with Jeju pork, glutinous rice, and condiments you add yourself to adjust the heat. Bigger spenders can go for the charcoal-finished Wagyu Beef Tongue ($58++) with bayam, a leafy vegetable also known as amaranth.
Image credit: JJAN
The 41-seat shophouse has a hanok-inspired interior with a painted dancheong ceiling, carved wooden brackets, and furniture made by craftsmen in Korea. It’s a six-minute walk from Maxwell and Tanjong Pagar MRT Stations .
In other Korean food news, check out our new Korean restaurants in Singapore guide . You can also read our guide to the best Korean cafes in Singapore .
Address: 45 Craig Road, Singapore 089683
Opening hours: Mon-Fri 5pm to 12am, Sat-Sun 1pm to 12am
Website
JJAN is not halal-certified.

Champagniac , Singapore’s dedicated Champagne festival, returns this weekend on 14 and 15 November for its second edition. It has moved from Jewel Changi Airport to the Supreme Court Terrace at National Gallery Singapore .
Credit: Champagniac 2025
Popping champagne in a former courthouse sounds like an objection, but I’m sure even lawyers won’t mind as long as their glasses are full.
Credit: National Gallery Singapore
Last year’s debut drew 1,400 people. The pitch hasn’t changed: Champagne for everyone, not only the person at dinner who smells “ brioche ” without being asked. Led by Yeo Xi Yang — he’s the 2022 Singapore National Sommelier Champion and runs Convivial , Southeast Asia’s first dedicated Champagne bar.
Champagne houses and growers pouring at Champagniac 2026
Credit: Champagniac 2025
For a festival trying to make Champagne more accessible, they’ve managed to bring in some seriously good producers. Big houses like Billecart-Salmon , Pommery , Deutz and Jacquesson sit alongside the growers Champagne nerds go misty-eyed over: Egly-Ouriet , Larmandier-Bernier , Pascal Doquet . Then there’s Selosse Pajon , made by the grand-nephew of Jacques Selosse and pouring in Singapore for the first time. If that surname means nothing to you, the queue at that booth will explain it.
There’s sparkling from outside Champagne, too. Gusbourne and Roebuck Estates are flying the English flag, and Spain’s Bodegas Balmoral is there with its traditional-method Edoné range. It’s a good chance to test whether you can tell English fizz from French. I wouldn’t bet money on it.
What the S$98 ticket covers
A regular ticket gets you one three-hour session, an SKLO Linear N.1 glass to take home (valued at S$69) and one tasting per booth. Note the “one.” Some of the highlighted bottles are premium pours, paid for with tokens sold on-site at S$5 each. The festival hasn’t published the token prices for individual bottles, so it’s hard to know how much extra you’ll end up spending.
Is the Champagniac VIP ticket worth it?
VIP is S$198 and capped at 60 people per session. What you’re really paying for is access to the Glass Room , a private lounge with seating and eight premium cuvées personally selected by Yeo. These are rarer bottles from houses at the fair that won’t be poured on the main floor. Three he’s flagged are the Egly-Ouriet V.P. Grand Cru , Henri Giraud MV20 Aÿ Grand Cru and Jacquesson Cuvée 743 .
For an extra S$100, that’s eight pours you won’t find elsewhere at the festival, plus somewhere to sit down. If you were already planning to burn through tokens, VIP makes sense. If you just want to discover a few new champagnes and have a good afternoon, the regular ticket is enough. VIPs can also pay another S$60 for the Grower package or S$80 for the Grande Maison package.
Credit: Champagniac 2025
Masterclasses, art and everything else
There are three masterclasses, each capped at 24 seats and booked separately on top of a festival ticket. On Saturday at 2.30pm, Alexandre Collard runs a Collard-Picard session (S$68), and everyone goes home with a demi-bottle. Sunday’s 2.30pm slot is Champagne A. Bergère, also S$68. The Henri Giraud class (S$88) is on Friday’s preview night, which is for National Gallery members only.
There’s also a Champagne-and-watercolour workshop with French artist D’Gers, where you get to paint your own postcard. It’s free for the first 30 people each session and S$10 after that. German artist Míru is showing new work, and three DJs are on the decks.
Buy your tickets to Champagniac 2026
Address: Supreme Court Terrace, Level 4, National Gallery Singapore, 1 St Andrew’s Road, Singapore 178957
Dates: 14–15 November 2026 (members’ preview on 13 November, 7pm–10pm)
Sessions: 11am–2pm & 4pm–7pm, both days
Ticket prices: S$98 (Regular) or S$198 (VIP), plus S$5 tokens and S$68–S$88 for masterclasses
*Every ticket includes an SKLO Linear N.1 tasting glass (worth $69)

Mister Donut has three Christmas donuts made with KitKat this year, sold at three for S$9.90 as a festive offer, or S$3.50 each at the usual price. The offer is for a limited time and while stocks last.
Two of the three are chewy donuts, and the third is a fluffy filled one.
The three KitKat donuts
• Holly Berry Wreath: a chewy ring dressed in strawberry chocolate, with a whole KitKat finger laid across the top.
• Frosty Choco Bauble: a fluffy donut filled with KitKat spread and wrapped in white chocolate, piped with red lines like a bauble.
• Merry Mint Garland: chewy donut halves filled with mint-infused KitKat spread and coated in mint chocolate.
Holly Berry Wreath, a chewy ring in strawberry chocolate with a KitKat finger. Image: Mister Donut Singapore
The Holly Berry Wreath contains wheat gluten, milk, soybean and egg, and no tree nut. The Frosty Choco Bauble and Merry Mint Garland both add tree nut, which matters for anyone buying a box for a children’s party.
Frosty Choco Bauble is filled with KitKat spread. Image: Mister Donut Singapore
Boxes and the donut tree stand
For orders, the chain’s online shop sells boxes of six at S$21. There is a box of each flavour and a Christmas Collection box with two of each.
There is also a Donut Tree Stand at S$8.80, a DIY tiered stand that holds 24 donuts.
The Donut Tree Stand costs S$8.80 and holds 24 donuts. Image: Mister Donut Singapore
Where to buy
Mister Donut, run in Singapore by RE&S, has 12 outlets: Anchorvale Village, Junction 8, Jurong Point, Northpoint City, Parkway Parade, Takashimaya Food Hall, Tampines 1, Thomson Plaza, Velocity@Novena Square, VivoCity, Waterway Point and 313@somerset. Most open from 11am to 9pm daily. Anchorvale Village is open from 11am to 9.30pm, Takashimaya Food Hall from 10am to 9.30pm, and VivoCity from 11am to 9.30pm on Monday to Thursday and from 10am to 10pm on Friday to Sunday.
Boxes and the tree stand are on order.misterdonut.com.sg for pickup or delivery.

deals.body:
Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is a Chinese-style mutton soup stall at 115 Bukit Merah View Food Centre , with eager customers already forming a queue before it even opens for the day. Erm, well, not quite for the whole day. It operates for just 2.5 hours (11am – 1.30pm) , 5 days a week . With a rating of 4.6 stars out of 5 with a total of 369 reviews (at time of writing), it’s Singapore’s highest-rated mutton soup stall on Google Reviews .
A little voice in my head went, “It must be pretty darn good, eh?” This stall has also been awarded a Michelin Bib Gourmand for 9 consecutive years — that alone speaks volumes.
Naturally, my expectations were much higher than usual. As I stood in the queue, a rhythmic chopping sound echoed through the air, accompanied by a lady calling out and taking customers’ orders. As the fast-moving line gradually inched closer, the sounds that had been teasing my ears finally came into full view. From a conversation I couldn’t help but overhear, I gathered that the 2 ladies take turns swapping roles.
What to order at Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang
Most of the menu items come in 5 sizes, ranging from S$6 to S$10 , so there’s something suitable for every appetite. Just like the local saying goes, “Monkey see, monkey do.” I followed the lead of those queuing ahead of me and ordered the S$8 portion of the 羊杂 (mixed mutton) with a small bowl of Rice (S$0.40) .
For the price, I must say, the portion is pretty generous. There were pieces of mutton, 5 lamb balls, and lamb’s stomach bathed in a light brown soup, garnished with chopped Chinese celery.
The moment the soup hit my tongue, I was greeted by an unusual tingling sensation, accompanied by an almost siap siap mouthfeel. Its robust herbal profile brought to mind a hearty bowl of bak kut teh . It was definitely an acquired taste, and those who dislike herbal flavours may not appreciate it much. As someone who doesn’t mind herbal soups, I still felt that the flavour could be toned down a little to suit a wider audience.
The mutton here has got to be the Wagyu of its kind because, OMG, the meat was so tender that it barely required chewing, There was also no trace of unpleasant gaminess.
The lamb balls were firm yet smooth, and the overall texture reminded me of bouncy fishballs. It also packed a great flavour which wasn’t overly floury.
The stomach pieces were impeccably prepared, with a pleasantly clean flavour and none of that funky offal taste. I even found a couple of pieces of honeycomb tripe.
I then moved on to the S$8 bowl of 羊排骨汤 (mutton ribs soup) with rice as well. For S$8 , you’ll get about 7 to 8 substantial pieces of ribs. Much like the mutton from the previous dish, the rib meat was beautifully soft, with a pleasing balance of fat and lean meat.
For chilli lovers, I must say that this one is gentle enough for those who can’t handle too much heat, with a tangy profile reminiscent of the chilli commonly served alongside orh luak .
Who Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is best for
It’s perfect for herbal soup lovers who love something comforting for lunch. For those who avoid mutton like the plague because of its potential gaminess, Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is a great place to start for its delicious, tender mutton; minus the strong taste.
How to get there?
115 Bukit Merah View Food Centre isn’t exactly near any MRT station. My recommendation would be to alight at Tiong Bahru MRT Station (EW17), get to the Opp Tiong Bahru Stn/Plaza bus stop, and board bus services that take you to Blk 116 .
Do we recommend Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang ?
If you love robust herbal flavours, then Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang will be up your alley. Mutton lovers who enjoy innards will appreciate the quality and softness of the lamb here. Oh, and I mustn’t forget the warm, friendly and efficient service here. It’s certainly the cherry on top!

HanBroth is a new Korean hawker stall in Beauty World
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
The weather’s been quite chilly recently, with seemingly never-ending rain. To me, that only means it’s time to snuggle up under a blanket, sip a cup of hot chocolate, and slurp on a comforting bowl of hot soup. If you’re anything like me, you’re in luck: MasterChef Singapore Season 2 winner Derek Cheong recently opened HanBroth , specialising in Busan-style pork bone soup, following the resounding success of sister stall Berempah Bros .
MasterChef Finalist Opens Ayam Berempah Stall At Beauty World—Here’s Our Honest Review
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
Dwaeji-gukbap, AKA Busan-style pork bone soup, is one of Busan’s iconic dishes, its name literally translating to “pork, soup, rice”. It originated during the Korean War in the 1950s, and is made by simmering pork bones for hours, resulting in a milky white broth best served with banchan, or Korean side dishes.
To replicate the flavours you’ll get in Busan, founder Derek Cheong scoured Korea’s best dwaeji-gukbap restaurants to learn more about the dish and bring the techniques back to Singapore. You can see that effort in how the dish is prepared: the broth is boiled for four to eight hours with pork femur bones, pork shank, trotters, pork belly, and pork collar, giving the soup a deep, porky flavour and a creamy, almost gelatinous finish.
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
Their best-seller is the Original Busan-Style Pork Soup ($9.90) , featuring their signature pork bone soup, served piping hot and packed with tender pork belly and pork collar. Each set also comes with a bowl of steamed rice, kimchi, ssamjang—a spicy Korean chilli sauce—a blend of salt and pepper, and dadaegi, which is a spicy house-made chilli paste.
The recommended way to eat it is to dump the whole bowl of rice into the soup, pao fan style. If you want to zhng up your broth, add a spoonful of the spicy-salty dadaegi paste and the salt-and-pepper blend. Season the pork by dipping it into ssamjang or pairing it with kimchi.
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
If you’re feeling under the weather, order their Herbal Busan-Style Pork Soup ($11.90) instead, spiked with ginseng, dates, and other Korean herbs for a samgyetang-like experience .
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
Their Seaweed Busan-style Pork Soup ($11.90) is another variant that’s made by boiling seaweed in the broth, which lends it a deep, umami, and briny taste.
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
That’s not all: they also have sides to share ‘round the table, including the Potato Pancake ($9.90) : a rosti-like potato pancake drizzled with smoked gochujang-flavoured and bonito-flavoured mayo, then finished with seaweed for additional crunch. The pancake is said to be crispy on the outside, while soft and fluffy on the inside.
Image credit: HANBROTH via Google Maps
Otherwise, their Pork Bossam ($9.90) is also highly popular. It comprises pork shoulder that’s simmered in an aromatic blend of garlic, Korean soybean paste, ginger, and more, served with wasabi, the same salt-and-pepper mix, and ssamjang. Online reviews have raved about it being tender yet not too fatty.
HanBroth is located in Bukit Timah Wet Market & Food Centre , a three-minute walk away from Beauty World MRT Station .
If you’re already in the area, 133 Penang Authentic is worth a visit too, a stall by another award-winning chef in the same hawker centre serving up affordable Penang food. You can also browse our guide to the best foods in Beauty World for more ideas.
Address: 2A Jalan Seh Chuan, #01-41, Bukit Timah Wet Market & Food Centre, Singapore 599213
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 2:30pm, 5:30pm to 8:30pm
Website
HanBroth is not halal-certified.

Sushi Express Christmas platters are coming to Singapore from 7 to 31 December 2026, and this year the festive spread is shaped like a tree. The conveyor-belt sushi chain is rolling out three tree-shaped sushi platters, priced from S$19, along with a plush mascot eco bag for app members.
The three Sushi Express Christmas tree platters (Image: Sushi Express)
Three Sushi Express Christmas tree platters
The platters are the star of the festive menu, each served in a Christmas tree-shaped tray. They scale up in size and price, so you can pick one for a solo treat or a family spread.
Twinkle Delight Platter (S$19)
The smallest of the trio features Hana Maki Sushi topped with three star-shaped tamago, which gives the tray its twinkling look.
Twinkle Delight Platter (Image: Sushi Express)
Joyful Noel Platter (S$25)
Made for sharing, the Joyful Noel Platter has Grilled Salmon perched at the peak of the tree.
Joyful Noel Platter (Image: Sushi Express)
Merry Forest Platter (S$30)
The biggest of the three is topped with salmon sashimi and offers the widest selection, so it is the one to order if you are feeding a crowd.
Merry Forest Platter (Image: Sushi Express)
Eco Bag Plush for app members
App members also get an exclusive Eco Bag Plush: a recyclable bag tucked inside a soft plush of mascot Shimizu Salmon-kun. It is a cute, practical keepsake that doubles as a reusable shopping bag.
The Eco Bag for app members (Image: Sushi Express)
Shimizu Salmon-kun Eco Bag Plush (Image: Sushi Express)
Where and when to get them
The Christmas offerings are available from 7 to 31 December 2026 at Sushi Express, Sushi Plus and 争鲜gogo outlets. They are for takeaway only, so plan to pick them up and bring them home for the party. Prices are as provided by the brand; check outlets or the Sushi Express app for availability.
It is a pocket-friendly alternative if you are planning a festive gathering on a budget. If you are collecting festive eats this season, you may also like The Orchard Cafe’s Christmas buffet and Mister Donut’s KitKat Christmas donuts . We also covered the chain’s earlier Minions-themed sushi menu .

Are you the kind of person who likes a no-frills meal in the midst of a busy work or school day, as long as it’s tasty and filling? Tsui Wah might have the answer for you – its new limited-time menu that embodies that spirit of a simple, delicious meal from a Hong Kong cha chaan teng .
Credit: Tsui Wah
The highlight is a series of new hearty rice meals for one , starting at S$13.80 , featuring generous portions of familiar ingredients for the perfect comfort meal . This includes the Baked Pork and Corn with Fried Rice in Cream Sauce (S$14.80) , affectionately known as “Show Me Your Love” for its Cantonese pronunciation.
Another timeless cha chaan teng staple in the new menu is Minced Beef with Pasteurised Egg and Steamed Rice (S$14.80) . The steamed rice is topped off with a golden-orange egg yolk, symbolising “Overflowing Love”.
Credit: Tsui Wah
Looking for a drink to complete your meal? There is also a selection of refreshing drinks, including the popular Red Bean and Green Tea/Vanilla Ice-Cream Float ($6.80) , and the new 7UP with Salted Lime ($5.80) and 7UP with Vanilla Ice-Cream ($5.80) .
If you noticed a little ‘love’ theme here, that’s because Tsui Wah launched the new menu items in conjunction with Singles’ Day (11.11) ! But whether you’re dining alone or with a special someone, you’ll probably find a meal that brightens your day.
Drop by your nearest Tsui Wah outlet and find out for yourself.
Tsui Wah

About 130 independent brands sell fashion, jewellery, beauty, kids' wear, pet goods and festive food and drink, with a grand Christmas tree, a train and hot air balloon installation and Santa. A 1-Day Pass is $8, two people pay $14 on the BFF Pass, the Multi-Day Pass is $14, and children 10 and under go free. Every ticket comes with a free Yeo's drink, MBS parking is capped at S$12.84 a day for ticket holders, and Grab code TCA2026 takes 15% off your ride (up to $3).

Food options at AEON Mall Tebrau City in JB are getting more variety, with several new eateries joining its line-up. From crispy British-style fish and chips and comforting Hong Kong noodles to Korean fried chicken and Singapore-style min jiang kueh , there’s plenty to look forward to on your next mall visit.
Here are 7 new F&B openings to check out at AEON Mall Tebrau City , JB .
1. BatterCatch (Now open – S23, Level 2)
Credit – BatterCatch
Seafood lovers can get their fix at BatterCatch , a Singaporean fish and chips chain with MUIS Halal certification . Specialising in British-style comfort food, its menu features golden-battered fish made with choices such as halibut, haddock and barramundi, served with fries, mushy peas and house-made sauces.
Beyond its signature fish and chips, you can also tuck into other mains like pasta, burgers, and pies.
2. Zok Noodle House (Now open – S26, Level 2)
Established in 2011, Zok Noodle House brings Hong Kong and Macau-inspired comfort food to the table, with an emphasis on quality ingredients and house recipes. Its signature dumpling noodles are a good starting point, alongside pork bone broth noodles in spicy or milky soup.
The extensive menu also covers curry noodles, spicy chilli rice noodles, wonton noodles and steamed dim sum , including shrimp dumplings, crab roe siu mai and golden custard buns. Rice dishes and other pork-based noodle combinations round out the selection.
3. Nasi Lemak Shop (Nov 2026)
KL’s popular Nasi Lemak Shop is expected to arrive in November, bringing its familiar nasi lemak fix to Johor Bahru. Look out for its Nasi Lemak Ayam Goreng Berempah , alongside sides such as Sambal Kerang . The menu also includes local favourites like Mee Siam , giving diners more than one reason to drop by.
4. NakNak (Dec 2026)
Credit – NakNak
Korean fast food fans can look forward to NakNak , which combines 100% beef burgers, fried chicken and loaded fries. Its Nak Dak Boneless Thigh comes coated in your choice of Soy Garlic, Spicy Gochujang or Cheese Sauce, while wings and drumettes offer more saucy options.
Burger choices include Cheeseburger , Spicy Double Cheeseburger and Mushroom Swiss , as well as chicken burgers. For a more indulgent bite, try the Spicy Gochujang Mozzarella NakDak Burger .
5. Munchi Pancakes (Dec 2026)
Credit – Munchi Pancakes
Singapore’s Munchi Pancakes is bringing over 20 flavours of min jiang kueh , or apam balik , to the mall. What started as a hawker stall in Yishun has grown into a brand with over 42 outlets across Singapore.
Alongside familiar fillings like Peanut , Coconut , Red Bean and Kaya , expect creative options such as Biscoff , Milo Dinosaur , Matcha , Thai Milk Tea and Pistachio Kunafa . Mini Munchi boxes come with 6 pieces , making it easier to sample a few flavours in one go.
6. Subway (Dec 2026)
Credit – Subway Malaysia
For a quick, customisable meal, Subway is also expected to open in December. Its menu spans 6-inch and footlong subs, wraps and salads, with familiar picks including Chicken Teriyaki , Roasted Chicken , Italian B.M.T. , Steak & Cheese , Meatball Marinara and Tuna . Egg Mayo and Veggie Delite are available for those after something simpler.
7. Pepper Lunch (Jan 2027)
Credit – Chonky the Shiba Woofer via Google Reviews
Sizzling hotplate meals are coming to AEON Mall Tebrau City with Pepper Lunch , the Japanese fast-casual chain known for its signature iron plates. Meals arrive piping hot, allowing diners to mix their ingredients and sauces as the meat continues cooking at the table.
Its popular Beef Pepper Rice combines thinly sliced beef, rice, sweet corn and black pepper, while other options include steak platters, chicken and salmon sets, hotplate pasta and Japanese curry.

Out with the old and in with the new — Tampines Mall has just completed its S$24 million Asset Enhancement Initiative (AEI). That’s essentially a revamp, and you can look forward to 21 new brands , refreshed retail spaces and upgraded facilities during your next visit. I believe more is more when it comes to a shopping mall, so these new shops will definitely give shoppers greater choice and a more rounded experience.
Credit – CapitaLand
Of the 21 brands introduced, 15 are new to the East. Additionally, with 14 beauty retail stores, Tampines Mall is now home to the biggest beauty cluster in the East. This includes well-known, premium brands and more accessible, everyday beauty names. The 8 new beauty brands are: CHANEL, DIOR, ELEMIS, Judydoll, Rituals, Sephora, SHISEIDO, and YSL Beauty. Besides the newbies on the block, the brands with refreshed looks are Bath & Body Works, Kiehl’s, L’Occitane, Laneige and The Body Shop.
Credit – CapitaLand
Beyond shopping until you drop, standalone boutiques on Level 1 offer distinctive personalised services . For example, SHISEIDO offers a personalised skin analysis for the best skincare and makeup recommendations.
A trip to Tampines Mall isn’t complete without having a meal; there are also 8 new F&B concepts . These dining spaces include Alchemist, Casa Vostra, Ging Sun Ho King of Bun, IM QALB by Pun Im, LONGJING, RUXU, YEAH Gelato and Charlie’s Tea. Don’t miss out on IM QALB’s Tampines Mall-exclusive menu. Plus, Charlie’s Tea’s Tampines Mall outlet is their first-ever in Singapore.
Credit – CapitaLand
Shop for a new wardrobe at 5 new fashion, sports and watch stores — Asics, Boarding Gate, Braun Buffel, Meileur Moment and CC Primos. Brands that have had a store makeover include Decathlon, Running Lab, Goldheart, SK Gold and Vincent Watch. Decathlon’s 18,000-square-foot store has more than 6,000 sporting essentials across over 60 different sports. You can try out various gear at dedicated test zones before committing to a purchase. Post-purchase services such as basic bicycle maintenance, racket restringing and re-gripping are also available.
I know where I’m heading this weekend, and I hope you do too!

Attention Westies! 505 Jurong West Market & Food Centre has just welcomed a new Korean addition to its hawkers. In the sea of stalls serving up traditional local fare, Busan Pork Soup ‘s unmistakable red signage stands out immediately. At the time of writing, Busan Pork Soup has yet to even be added to Google Maps, so we’ve got the full lowdown for you right here.
Credit – Busan Pork Soup via IG
As per the name, Busan Pork Soup specialises in Korean pork soup, otherwise known as dwaeji-gukbap . The stall is from the same team behind OMMA Chicken Soup, which operates multiple outlets islandwide. Similar to their sister brand, the soup recipes served at Busan Pork Soup are crafted by the same 2 chefs who formerly worked in a Michelin-starred Korean restaurant before bringing their signature Korean fare to the Singaporean hawker scene.
The menu centres around unbelievably tender pork slices and their signature 10-hour slow-simmered broth. No MSG is added to the broth, so all the rich and savoury flavours are extracted solely from the pork itself.
Each bowl comes in 3 sizes, with varying amounts of pork slices. Small gets you 3 slices, while medium gets 4 and large gets 5.
Credit – Busan Pork Soup
Menu highlights include their bestselling Tomato Busan (S$6.90 for small) , which comes with 3 slices of melt-in-your-mouth pork and steaming-hot savoury tomato and pork broth.
For kimchi lovers, order the Kimchi Busan (S$7.30 for small) to hit that spicy-sour craving. If you prefer something on the milder side, go for the Collagen Busan (S$6.50 for small) for a comforting, milky-white broth.
Sides and add-ons like Kimchi (S$1.50) , Short Grain Rice (S$0.80) and Quail Egg (S$1.50) are also available amongst others.
If you’re looking to get your soupy Korean fix, consider supporting this brand-new stall down in Jurong!
Ex-Michelin star restaurant chefs sell Korean samgyetang from $6.80 at hawker stalls

deals.body:
Best food places to use CDC Vouchers
With over 24,000 local establishments accepting CDC Vouchers as of June 2026, you’re spoiled for choice when it comes to deciding where to makan. But don’t worry, we’ve curated a bunch of the best food places for you, be it cafes, restaurants, fruit stalls, or bakeries to spend your SG60 and CDC Vouchers. There’s something on this list for every tastebud.
Cafes
1. Hello Arigato
Hello Arigato is best known for its stacked Japanese-inspired sando, including the crowd-favourite Gyu Sando ($28++) , which stars a thick slab of beef tenderloin katsu and house-made caramelised onion jam. The Pork Katsu Sando ($24++) is another hearty pick that’s equally satisfying. Wash it all down with their Strawberry Matcha Cloud ($6.50++) , a light and refreshing drink that hits the spot on a sweltering day.
They’ve got five outlets in Singapore, but to use your CDC Vouchers, head to the Everton Park , Joo Chiat , and Tiong Bahru ones.
Read our Hello Arigato feature .
Everton Park outlet
Address: 4 Everton Park, #01-42, Singapore 080004
Opening hours: Tue-Fri 9am to 5pm, Sat-Sun 8am to 5pm
Joo Chiat outlet
Address: 314 Joo Chiat Road, Singapore 427565
Opening hours: Mon-Fri 9am to 5pm, Sat-Sun 8am to 5pm
Tiong Bahru outlet
Address: 58 Seng Poh Road, #01-15, Singapore 160058
Opening hours: Mon-Fri 8am to 4pm, Sat-Sun 8am to 5pm
Website
Hello Arigato is not halal-certified.
Hello Arigato Opens In Tiong Bahru With Orh Nee Coffee, Cai Poh Egg Sando And More
2. Bag Me Up Bagel House
Bag Me Up Bagel House has quickly become a neighbourhood favourite since opening in Everton Park in late 2022, drawing crowds with their house-made bagels. Their menu features eight different bagels: four signature creations (from $10.50) and four lighter options ($6.50) for smaller appetites.
Top picks include the cheekily named Can’t Trust Chick ($14.50) , stuffed with grilled teriyaki chicken, sautéed mushrooms, truffle schmear, and melty mozzarella, and the breakfast-inspired Brekkie ($12.50) , layered with caramelised beef bacon, scrambled eggs, torched cheddar, pickles, and their house sauce. Pair your bagel with one of their protein smoothies ($11.90) for a satisfying meal that’ll fuel your day.
Read our Bag Me Up Bagel House review .
Address: 2 Everton Park, #01-59B, Singapore 081002
Opening hours: Tue, Sat-Sun 9am to 3pm, Wed-Fri 9:30am to 3pm
Website
Bag Me Up is not halal-certified.
Bag Me Up Review: Unagi And Wagyu Beef Bagels At This Under HDB Bagel Shop Near Outram Park
3. Cafe Fufu
Tucked away under an HDB block in Redhill, Cafe Fufu isn’t just your usual minimalist brunch spot—it’s actually a wood-fired pizzeria. There are plenty of options on the menu, but if you need a recommendation, try their signature Pizza Fufu ($20+ for personal, $30+ for sharing) . It swaps out the usual tomato base for a fragrant coriander pesto, and comes topped with fresh tiger prawns, semi-dried tomatoes, and a dusting of chilli flakes for a subtle kick.
Read our Cafe Fufu feature .
Address: 63B Lengkok Bahru, #01-362, Singapore 152063
Opening hours: Tue-Thurs 11am to 9pm, Fri 11am to 10pm, Sat 9am to 10pm, Sun 9am to 4pm
Website
Cafe Fufu is not halal-certified.
This Under-HDB Cafe In Redhill Has Wood-Fired Pizza And Tiramisu
4. Dearborn
Image: @dearborn.granola
Dearborn has only a few items on their menu—and that’s how you know they’re doing it well. This quiet little granola cafe tucked away in Everton Park whips up granola bowls (from $7) , served with your choice of dairy-free Raglan Coconut Vanilla Bean Yogurt , Delta Greek Yogurt, or Oatside Oat Milk. Flavours rotate between classics such as Strawberry Macadamia , Dark Chocolate Hazelnut Sea Salt , and a flavour of the day.
If you’re not feeling like a bowl, their house-made Sourdough with Dearborn butter (from $5) is worth a try too, with options including country or smoked cheddar and chilli. Swing by on a Saturday for a slightly expanded menu with off-menu specials.
Address: 1 Everton Park, #01-29, Singapore 081001
Opening hours: Mon-Fri 9am to 5pm, Sat-Sun 9am to 3pm
Website
Dearborn Granola is not halal-certified.
5. Cafe Wabi Sabi
Another gem in Everton Park is Cafe Wabi Sabi , a cosy Japanese cafe that’s just a 10-minute walk from Outram Park MRT Station . The menu leans into comfort food, with sando, soba, and donburi on rotation.
A must-try is the Pork Katsu Sando ($13.90++) , their bestseller. It features house-made shokupan stuffed with a thick slab of pork katsu, crisp salad, tomato, and cucumber. If you’re in the mood for a rice bowl, the Buta Don ($18.90++) is another solid pick, served with braised Iberico pork, caramelised onions, shimeji mushrooms, and tangy pickles.

Bag Me Up Bagel House has quickly become a neighbourhood favourite since opening in Everton Park in late 2022, drawing crowds with their house-made bagels. Their menu features eight different bagels: four signature creations (from $10.50) and four lighter options ($6.50) for smaller appetites.
Top picks include the cheekily named Can’t Trust Chick ($14.50) , stuffed with grilled teriyaki chicken, sautéed mushrooms, truffle schmear, and melty mozzarella, and the breakfast-inspired Brekkie ($12.50) , layered with caramelised beef bacon, scrambled eggs, torched cheddar, pickles, and their house sauce. Pair your bagel with one of their protein smoothies ($11.90) for a satisfying meal that’ll fuel your day.
Read our Bag Me Up Bagel House review .
Address: 2 Everton Park, #01-59B, Singapore 081002
Opening hours: Tue, Sat-Sun 9am to 3pm, Wed-Fri 9:30am to 3pm
Website
Bag Me Up is not halal-certified.
Bag Me Up Review: Unagi And Wagyu Beef Bagels At This Under HDB Bagel Shop Near Outram Park
3. Cafe Fufu
Tucked away under an HDB block in Redhill, Cafe Fufu isn’t just your usual minimalist brunch spot—it’s actually a wood-fired pizzeria. There are plenty of options on the menu, but if you need a recommendation, try their signature Pizza Fufu ($20+ for personal, $30+ for sharing) . It swaps out the usual tomato base for a fragrant coriander pesto, and comes topped with fresh tiger prawns, semi-dried tomatoes, and a dusting of chilli flakes for a subtle kick.
Read our Cafe Fufu feature .
Address: 63B Lengkok Bahru, #01-362, Singapore 152063
Opening hours: Tue-Thurs 11am to 9pm, Fri 11am to 10pm, Sat 9am to 10pm, Sun 9am to 4pm
Website
Cafe Fufu is not halal-certified.

4. Dearborn
Image: @dearborn.granola
Dearborn has only a few items on their menu—and that’s how you know they’re doing it well. This quiet little granola cafe tucked away in Everton Park whips up granola bowls (from $7) , served with your choice of dairy-free Raglan Coconut Vanilla Bean Yogurt , Delta Greek Yogurt, or Oatside Oat Milk. Flavours rotate between classics such as Strawberry Macadamia , Dark Chocolate Hazelnut Sea Salt , and a flavour of the day.
If you’re not feeling like a bowl, their house-made Sourdough with Dearborn butter (from $5) is worth a try too, with options including country or smoked cheddar and chilli. Swing by on a Saturday for a slightly expanded menu with off-menu specials.
Address: 1 Everton Park, #01-29, Singapore 081001
Opening hours: Mon-Fri 9am to 5pm, Sat-Sun 9am to 3pm

5. Cafe Wabi Sabi
Another gem in Everton Park is Cafe Wabi Sabi , a cosy Japanese cafe that’s just a 10-minute walk from Outram Park MRT Station . The menu leans into comfort food, with sando, soba, and donburi on rotation.
A must-try is the Pork Katsu Sando ($13.90++) , their bestseller. It features house-made shokupan stuffed with a thick slab of pork katsu, crisp salad, tomato, and cucumber. If you’re in the mood for a rice bowl, the Buta Don ($18.90++) is another solid pick, served with braised Iberico pork, caramelised onions, shimeji mushrooms, and tangy pickles.

Si Yan Teochew Dining opened on Friday, 13 November 2026, in the basement of Palais Renaissance on Orchard Road. The restaurant takes units #B1-01 to #B1-03 and builds its menu around Teochew seafood, from marinated crab to oyster omelette, with dim sum at lunch.
For the opening, Si Yan members pay soft-opening prices on three signature dishes, which the restaurant calls the Si Yan Signature Trio, until 3 January 2027. Membership is free to join.
The members’ prices, dish by dish
• Signature Teochew Style Shark’s Fin in Supreme Broth, served in a Japanese stone pot: S$38, down from S$58
• Braised 3-Head Australian Abalone in Abalone Sauce: S$38 a piece, down from S$62
• Alaskan King Crab Steamed with Chinese Wine: S$14 per 100g, down from S$28 per 100g, by advance order only
The prices run daily at lunch and dinner, for dine-in in the main dining hall only. Membership is required, the offer cannot be combined with other promotions, vouchers or membership benefits, and the dishes are subject to availability. GST and service charge come on top.
How membership works
Anyone aged 18 and above can sign up for Si Yan membership online at no cost, with one account per person. It lasts 12 months and renews for S$3 a year, paid in person at the restaurant. Members show their membership before paying.
New members get a S$10 welcome voucher that activates 24 hours after sign-up and lasts 90 days, and earn SY$1 for every S$10 spent on regular-priced à la carte food. The voucher cannot be used together with the opening prices, since those exclude vouchers.
Double-Boiled Pineapple Kampong Chicken Soup with Pig Stomach, an advance-order dish. Photo: Si Yan Teochew Dining
What else is on the menu
The kitchen leans on an aged ingredient: 15-year vintage preserved turnip, or chai poh. It goes into a stir-fried XO carrot cake at S$16 and a wok-fried hor fun with crispy pork lard and XO sauce at S$28.
The oyster omelette is pan-fried whole into one crisp golden sheet rather than served loose, at S$24, with a prawn version at S$26. The kitchen asks for at least 40 minutes for either.
For a group, the Teochew Style Fresh Prawn Poached Rice with Crispy Rice comes in a claypot for four at S$58, and a whole roasted suckling pig is S$338 by advance order. The braised section covers duck, pork belly, trotters and beef shank, with a braised duo platter from S$32.
Teochew Style Fresh Prawn Poached Rice with Crispy Rice, S$58 for four. Photo: Si Yan Teochew Dining
Advance orders also cover the Teochew Marinated Red Cream Mud Crab, steeped in a house sauce for more than eight hours, and a double-boiled soup of pineapple enzyme-fed kampong chicken with a whole pig stomach cooked inside the bird.
Teochew Marinated Red Cream Mud Crab, marinated for more than eight hours. Photo: Si Yan Teochew Dining
Dim sum at lunch
Lunchtime dim sum starts at S$8.80 a basket, for items such as the Teochew glutinous rice roll, deep-fried taro puffs and BBQ honey pork buns. Prawn ha kao and siew mai are S$9.80. Teochew porridge with oyster and minced meat, or with dried scallop, is S$11.80 a person.
Until 30 November, members who spend at least S$50 on à la carte food at lunch (11am to 3pm) get 50% off all dim sum, with no limit on how many baskets they order. Dim sum and drinks do not count towards the S$50.
Hours and bookings
Si Yan Teochew Dining is at 390 Orchard Road, #B1-01, #B1-02/02A/03, Palais Renaissance, Singapore 238871, a short walk from Orchard Boulevard MRT station (TE13).
• Monday to Friday: 11am to 3pm (last order 2.30pm), 6pm to 10.30pm (last order 10pm)
• Saturday: 11am to 3.30pm (last order 3pm), 6pm to 10.30pm (last order 10pm)
• Sunday and public holidays: 10.30am to 3.30pm (last order 3pm), 6pm to 10.30pm (last order 10pm)
Reservations go through 6224 9088, WhatsApp on 8281 8188 or online booking . The full menus are on Si Yan’s website . Menu prices are before service charge and GST.

Tucked away in an industrial estate right next to the MRT tracks in Aljunied is An La Ghien -5 , a low-key spot serving genuine, home-style Vietnamese fare from 11am all the way to 5am, making it the perfect late-night supper spot.
Founded in 2019 by Yuki, a Vietnamese immigrant in Singapore who missed the taste of home, An La Ghien -5 has since been sharing authentic Vietnamese flavours with expatriates and locals alike.
Unlike Singapore’s more commercialised Vietnamese chains, the focus here is squarely on comforting, traditional cooking. Even better, they offer a wide variety of free-flow fresh herbs to customise your meal — a Vietnamese dining touch rarely seen anywhere else on the island. I mean, look at that fridgeful of greens!
What to order at An La Ghien -5
I came here specifically for the Sliced Beef Pho (S$3.90++) . While it is a fairly standard rendition, you get a remarkably generous portion of sliced beef for the price.
The clear beef broth is clean-tasting with a subtle sweetness, paired with flat white noodles that lean slightly softer than I would prefer.
Most of the beef slices were tender, though a few pieces turned out a touch dry and firm. Tossing in the fresh herbs really helped to elevate the bowl — I went with sprigs of basil and sawtooth coriander, which added a bright, almost peppery lift to the soup.
10 best Vietnamese food places in Singapore that will blow your mind
Next I dug into the Grilled Pork Chop and Vegetables with Rice Vermicelli (S$12.90++) . This turned out to be my favourite dish here, just for how fresh and light it was, thanks to the abundance of vegetables and herbs.
The pork chop in this dish was well-seasoned and had a nice char to it, adding just a hint of smokiness. It was moist and tender throughout and wasn’t dry or tough at any point. I found it to be a little salty on its own, but when enjoyed together with the noodles and vegetables, the saltiness is just right.
The small pile of pickled water spinach added a slight tang to the bowl and paired well with the grilled pork by helping to cut through its richness.
The noodles in this dish were similarly soft, though tossing them with the crisp lettuce created a great textural contrast that made every bite much more addictive. I particularly liked the accompanying sweet chilli sauce. Infused with fish sauce, it delivered a savoury umami depth alongside a gentle spicy kick without ever leaning overly sweet.
The menu also featured less common Vietnamese dishes such as Pan-Seared Goat Ribs (S$29.90) and Fried Frog Feet with Fish Sauce (S$14.90) that I’d definitely be interested in trying next time. They also specialise in hotpot and BBQ sets, making it ideal for communal meals or family dinners.
Who is An La Ghien -5 best for?
An La Ghien -5 is ideal for anyone craving authentic, home-style Vietnamese fare. And with doors staying open until 5am, it also doubles as a perfect supper spot in the East, offering a comforting meal after hours. Plus, if you love fresh herbs, the generous free-flow spread makes it easy to customise every bowl just the way you like it.
How to get to An La Ghien -5
An La Ghien -5 is located along Lorong 23 Geylang, which is just a 2-minute walk from Aljunied MRT station (EW9) . The station connects to the East-West line of the MRT. Use Exit A and cross Aljunied Road before continuing toward Lorong 23 Geylang.
If you prefer to travel by bus, you can stop at bus stop Opp Aljunied Stn (81081) and walk towards Lorong 23 Geylang. Do note that buses 158A and 125A only operate on weekdays.
Do we recommend An La Ghien -5 ?
The free-flow herbs are a massive plus if you enjoy bright, herbaceous flavours as much as I do. Coupled with an air-conditioned dining space, it makes for a comfortable meal. While the rest of the menu is priced slightly higher than the wallet-friendly S$3.90 pho , it remains a solid spot I would likely revisit whenever I am in the area, or craving a late-night supper.

Pavilion KL in Bukit Bintang has been welcoming a fresh mix of names to its retail lineup. The latest additions span artisan sourdough pastries, Michelin-starred Sichuan cuisine, niche fragrances and international fashion labels, with several highly anticipated brands also preparing to make their Malaysian debut.
Here are 18 new openings at Pavilion KL worth knowing about , including those arriving in the coming months.
Now open
1. adough (Level 3)
Credit – adough
Sourdough enthusiasts have another reason to visit Pavilion KL, as adough has opened its third bakery and cafe outlet here. Known for its artisan sourdough bakes, the menu features treats such as Pistachio Frangipane Croissants , Honey Butter Shio Pan , Pistachio Pain Suisse and seasonal fruit tarts.
There are savoury options too, including Spring Onion & Cheese Croissants , Jalapeño Seaweed Rolls and Chicken Pot Pies . Look out for its sourdough loaves, including Marmite & Cheese and Garlic , Rosemary & Sea Salt Focaccia , alongside cafe favourites like Matcha Brownies and Banana Chocolate Cake .
2. Burberry Beauty (Level 3)
Credit – Burberry
Burberry Beauty has opened its first flagship in Malaysia, bringing the British fashion house’s signature aesthetic into fragrance and make-up. Inspired by London’s character and the brand’s heritage, its collection features sophisticated scents and make-up essentials that balance classic elegance with a contemporary edge.
3. TROVE (Level 3)
Credit – TROVE
Beauty enthusiasts looking beyond mainstream labels can explore TROVE , a curated beauty and lifestyle store carrying niche fragrances, skincare, haircare and home essentials. Its fragrance selection includes Essential Parfums , Chasing Scents , D’Annam , The House of Oud and Ormonde Jayne , with full-sized bottles, discovery sets and travel-sized options available.

links.title: IKEA’s Christmas Buffet Is Back For Just $29.90—Here’s What To Expect
IKEA Singapore Brings Back Real Christmas Trees at $135, Plus Festive Meals from $15.90
IKEA Singapore Brings Back Real Christmas Trees at $135, Plus Festive Meals from $15.90

members.body:
IKEA’s Christmas buffet is returning in December
Image credit: IKEA
IKEA Singapore is part of some of my fondest memories. Growing up, it’s been my family’s favourite weekend dinner spot, and their meatballs are still one of my favourite childhood bites. If you’re an IKEA meatball enthusiast like me, I come bearing good news: IKEA’s buffet is back in anticipation of the Christmas season, featuring a spread of traditional Swedish Christmas buffet dishes.
The standout this time round is the Beef Goulash With Carrots and Potatoes , a hearty Hungarian stew made by simmering beef, carrots, potatoes, onions, and other aromatics, such as paprika, in a tomato-based broth. The result is a comforting, slightly smoky soup that’s best eaten with bread.
Image credit: IKEA
Europe’s long been known for its cheeses, and Sweden is no exception, so it’s only right to try IKEA’s Hushallsost Cheese , a traditional Swedish cow’s-milk cheese. For the uninitiated, it’s a semi-hard cheese made from cow’s whole milk, with a mild taste and subtle flavours of clear salt and fresh acidity. Due to its creamy texture and high fat content, it’s best savoured with Rye & Multigrain Crispbread .
Of course, you can’t leave without a plate of their iconic Swedish meatballs with Cream Sauce , made from a blend of beef and pork, and served with their signature cream sauce and lingonberry jam. For those who can’t eat pork or beef, get their Plant Balls with Cream Sauce instead, a vegetarian option with the same garnishes. From my years of experience at IKEA Food Market, both are best enjoyed with the Mashed Potatoes and Penne Pasta with Tomato Sauce .
Image credit: IKEA
To round off the meal, get their new festive desserts: the Belgium Chocolate Log Cake and Lingonberry Vanilla Log Cake . The former is a fan favourite, featuring a soft, fluffy sponge cake filled with indulgent chocolate buttercream, while the other is a fruity variant, with prominent notes of lingonberry and vanilla.
IKEA Singapore’s Christmas buffet is available at their three outlets for just $29.90++ per adult . Unfortunately, tickets for their Jurong and Alexandra outlets have sold out. However, ticket sales for their Tampines outlet will start on 17 November 2026 , so set your alarms if you wish to snag some of those prized tickets.
Image credit: IKEA
If you’ve missed the date, fret not; IKEA is also introducing some new festive dishes on their regular menu. From now till 3 January 2027 , you can order their Rosemary Chicken Set ($18.70++) : a whole chicken leg seasoned with rosemary, and served with a vegetable medley of broccoli, carrots, and edamame, plus mashed potatoes and cream sauce. The set also comes with a bowl of mushroom soup and a mini Christmas log cake. Then there’s the Boneless Pork Knuckle Set ($27.70++) , which features a roasted pork knuckle served with mashed potatoes and cream sauce. The pork is said to be tender on the inside, with a satisfyingly crunchy exterior. There is also the aforementioned Mini Christmas Log Cake ($4.90++) and a Christmas Cold Plate ($7.90++) , the latter comprising slices of smoked salmon, honey-baked ham, shrimp, and more.
If you’re looking for more buffets for this coming holiday season, read our guide to 1-for-1 buffet deals in 2026 . Otherwise, check out Cedele’s new Christmas menu for a Nordic-inspired Christmas spread.
Website | Full list of outlets
IKEA is not halal-certified.

Beauty World Food Centre guide
Whenever I step onto Level 4 of Beauty World Centre , the first thing that hits me is the smoky aroma drifting through the air, mingling with the unmistakable bustle of Beauty World Food Centre . Serving generations of diners since 1984, it remains one of Singapore’s most underrated hawker centres in my eyes, home to a diverse mix of cuisines, ranging from old-school stalwarts to newer names bringing fresh picks to the table. Here are the best Beauty World Food Centre stalls for those who can’t decide what to eat there.
30 Beauty World Food Gems Including DIY Okonomiyaki, Famous Eng Kee Wings And More
1. Berempah Bros
One of the newer stalls making waves at the food centre is Berempah Bros , helmed by MasterChef Singapore Season 2 finalist Derek Cheong. Best known for its creative take on ayam goreng berempah AKA spiced fried chicken with rice, the stall gives the familiar favourite a contemporary refresh while retaining its bold flavours.
You have to try their signature Ayam Berempah ($7.50) , which features a piece of deep-fried chicken with a crisp exterior that gives way to juicy, tender meat marinated in a fragrant blend of spices, with distinct notes of cumin and garlic. The chicken is topped with their signature “typhoon shelter crumbs”—a savoury mix of fried garlic, breadcrumbs, and a touch of chilli. Accompanying it is a serving of fragrant coconut rice infused with coconut milk and chicken stock, while a side of tangy achar and house-made sambal belacan rounds out the dish.
Read our Berempah Bros review .
Unit number: #04-51
Opening hours: Daily 10am to 9pm
Tel: 9058 9674
Website
Beramaph Bros is not halal-certified.
MasterChef Finalist Opens Ayam Berempah Stall At Beauty World—Here’s Our Honest Review
2. Top 1 Home Made Noodle
Image credit: @wreckmytummy
Seeing “Top 1” in its name may strike some as a little gimmicky, but Top 1 Home Made Noodle has earned its reputation over the years. The humble stall has been serving handmade noodles at the hawker centre since 1989, building a loyal following through its consistent craftsmanship.
The stall operates on a build-your-own-bowl concept, where diners begin by choosing from seven types of handmade noodles, including Mee Hoon Kueh , U-Mian , and Ban Mian . Next, pick your preferred soup base— Soup ($4.50) , Dry ($5) , Mala Soup ($5) , or Tom Yum ($5) —before customising your bowl with add-ons such as White Fish (+$1) , Salmon (+$1.50) , Fish Maw (+$2) , or Meatballs . The noodles are known for their springy, chewy texture, cooked just right with a pleasant bite without that overly doughy consistency.
Unit number: #04-51
Opening hours: Thur to Tue 11am to 5pm
Top 1 Home Made Noodle is not halal-certified.
3. Pink Candy
With the Korean wave in Singapore still going strong, you do not have to break the bank every time a craving strikes, as Pink Candy is one hawker stall worth checking out for affordable Korean fare. Established by a native Korean who has run the stall for over a decade, the eatery stands out in its corner of the hawker centre with its distinctive pink-themed decor and vibrant displays.
Diners are often spoilt for choice here with an extensive menu featuring over 40 items, many of which are your typical Korean favourites. This includes your typical Kimbap ($8.50) , Black Bean Noodles ($12.90) , Spicy Cold Beef Noodles ($14.90) , Bibimbab ($12.90) , and Spicy Rice Cake ($12.90) . If you are dining in larger groups, get their Pork Army Stew ($34.90) , Kimchi Pancake ($21.90) and Original Sweet-Spicy Fried Chicken ($36).
Unit number: #04-51
Opening hours: Wed to Mon 10:30am to 2:30pm, 5pm to 9:30pm, Tue 5pm to 9:30pm
Website
Pink Candy is not halal-certified.
4. Lao Gai Mee
Image credit: Mr Yang via Google Maps
It’s not easy to find kolo mee in Singapore, let alone a good one. Fans of the dish will likely be familiar with Lao Gai Mee , a stall run by young Malaysian hawkers serving traditional Kuching- and Sarawak-style noodles. The menu features four main options— Fish Ball Bak Chor ($5) , Kolo Mee ($5) , Char Siu Mee ($5.50) , and Sarawak Laksa ($6.50) , with a choice of Kolo Mee or thick bee hoon available for all dishes.
Their Kolo Mee comes topped with a generous serving of minced pork, char siew, crispy pork lard, and springy noodles tossed in a fragrant blend of shallot oil and rendered lard that gives the dish its signature savoury flavour. The noodles are perfectly chewy and satisfyingly QQ, all while being priced very reasonably. For an extra bite, add a side of fishballs ($1.20) , which provide a pleasant bounce to the meal.
Unit number: #04-41
Opening hours: Daily 8am to 8pm
Website
Lao Gai Mee is not halal-certified.
5. Xiang Xiang Ji

deals.body:
It’s the end of an era for Assam laksa lovers. Popular regional chain D’Laksa is officially winding down operations, pulling out of Singapore after almost 10 years of serving up its signature tangy mackerel-packed Assam laksa . As a farewell treat, D’Laksa is also running a Buy-2-Get-1-Free promotion at its last outlet at Compass One before permanently shuttering on 23 Nov 2026 .
Originally hailing from Johor Bahru, D’Laksa was known for offering the less common Penang-style laksa, which forgoes the more usual coconut milk base in favour of a robust, spicy fish-based broth. The brand built a loyal following through its quick-service kiosks nestled inside neighbourhood malls and food courts (including past spots like YewTee Point and Northpoint City).
Their signature dish of Asam Laksa (S$6) comes with a generous portion of lettuce, pineapple and fish, giving the dish a tart aroma thanks to the sweet, sour and tangy flavours it packs. Their special prawn paste complements the sour tamarind sauce with its heavily umami profile. They also offer Asam Lobsterball (S$4.50) , which comes with 5 pieces of bouncy lobster balls drenched in their signature Assam sauce.
Credit – D’Laksa
Alternatively, try their Asam Pedas Stingray with Rice (S$8.90) , which features a slab of stingray meat dressed in a bold, spicy gravy. Sides and beverages such as Fruit Rojak (S$5.50) and Cendol Drink (S$2.50) are also available.
While the brand has steadily scaled back its islandwide footprint over recent months, this quiet closure marks the end of D’Laksa in Singapore, with only their Johor Bahru outlets remaining. Fans of D’Laksa should head down to Compass One before 23 Nov to enjoy the Buy-2-Get-1-Free deal and get one last bowl of their favourite Penang-style Assam Laksa; otherwise, you’ll have to trek across the border to get a taste.
Traditional Penang Food: Authentic Penang assam laksa, fried kway teow, Nyonya fried rice & chendol in Toa Payoh
