Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee is a nearly 4-decade-old Michelin-recognised institution which has been serving handmade fishballs and Teochew-style noodles in Pasar 16 @ Bedok . For any foodies hunting down old-school hawker fare in the East, this stall is a must-visit for the decades of heritage it brings to the table.
As rare as handmade fishballs are, handmade fishballs made from ikan parang are even harder to come across. I kan parang is bony and difficult to process into fishballs and most stalls use yellowtail instead. Stepping up to a stall that goes the extra mile immediately had me excited to try their fare.
What to order at Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee
I opted for Dry Fishball Noodles with Mee Pok (S$4) to enjoy at the hawker centre, and got the Fishball Noodle Soup with Kway Teow (S$4) along with an extra side of Fishball Soup (S$7) to-go.
One serving of Dry Fishball Noodles gets you a generous portion of your noodles of choice, a bowl of clear soup containing 5 precious fishballs and 1 her giao , a traditional Teochew fish dumpling.
The fishballs are definitely the highlight for me. They possess a satisfying bounce and irregular shaping, all telltale signs of a handmade fishball. They possess a naturally sweet flavour from the flesh of ikan parang , and you can tell that not much filler is used as the fishballs don’t have that flour-heavy, starchy bite that commercial surimi fishballs are often guilty of.
When bitten, it breaks apart in tender layers of flesh. It’s quite minimally seasoned so the flavour of the fresh fish meat really shines through. The her giao differs texturally with a firmer, chewier texture and is distinctly less sweet than the fishballs.
The soup was similarly lightly seasoned and contained bits of preserved vegetables which gave it a slight salty finish, which complemented the subtle sweetness of the fishballs well.
Mei Ling Fishball Noodle Showdown: Xin Lu Teochew Fishball Noodles vs Hup Kee Teochew Fishball Noodles
Unfortunately, the mee pok noodles were a little disappointing. I opted for the spicy version, which had the perfect kick and a good balance of sweet and savoury. Sadly, the noodles were quite alkaline-tasting and the sauce didn’t cling but had a clumpy, gummy texture. On the bright side, it was an extremely generous portion and quite filling.
If I came back, I’d recommend either skipping or getting a small portion of noodles and filling up on more fishballs.
As for the Fishball Noodle Soup with Kway Teow , it features the same amount of handmade fishballs and her giao as the dry version, but with flat, white rice noodles in the soup instead.
Disclaimer: If the fishballs look extra plentiful in this photo, that’s because I combined the noodles with the S $7 Fishball Soup, which comes with more fishballs and her giao than the standard S$ 4 bowl!
As I had them to-go, the noodles had soaked up the soup by the time I got home and became quite soft, easily breaking apart when I held them up with chopsticks. Texturally, it wasn’t too bad and was able to retain some chew despite the long journey home.
Who is Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee best for?
I can imagine Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee being best for handmade fishball purists who appreciate labour-intensive ikan parang fishballs. With how rare such fishballs are, I’d highly recommend this stall to anyone looking to try the real deal before it disappears from the hawker scene entirely. The stall is also ideal for those with larger appetites who prefer generous portions of filling noodles.

members.body:
Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee is a nearly 4-decade-old Michelin-recognised institution which has been serving handmade fishballs and Teochew-style noodles in Pasar 16 @ Bedok . For any foodies hunting down old-school hawker fare in the East, this stall is a must-visit for the decades of heritage it brings to the table.
As rare as handmade fishballs are, handmade fishballs made from ikan parang are even harder to come across. I kan parang is bony and difficult to process into fishballs and most stalls use yellowtail instead. Stepping up to a stall that goes the extra mile immediately had me excited to try their fare.
What to order at Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee
I opted for Dry Fishball Noodles with Mee Pok (S$4) to enjoy at the hawker centre, and got the Fishball Noodle Soup with Kway Teow (S$4) along with an extra side of Fishball Soup (S$7) to-go.
One serving of Dry Fishball Noodles gets you a generous portion of your noodles of choice, a bowl of clear soup containing 5 precious fishballs and 1 her giao , a traditional Teochew fish dumpling.
The fishballs are definitely the highlight for me. They possess a satisfying bounce and irregular shaping, all telltale signs of a handmade fishball. They possess a naturally sweet flavour from the flesh of ikan parang , and you can tell that not much filler is used as the fishballs don’t have that flour-heavy, starchy bite that commercial surimi fishballs are often guilty of.
When bitten, it breaks apart in tender layers of flesh. It’s quite minimally seasoned so the flavour of the fresh fish meat really shines through. The her giao differs texturally with a firmer, chewier texture and is distinctly less sweet than the fishballs.
The soup was similarly lightly seasoned and contained bits of preserved vegetables which gave it a slight salty finish, which complemented the subtle sweetness of the fishballs well.
Mei Ling Fishball Noodle Showdown: Xin Lu Teochew Fishball Noodles vs Hup Kee Teochew Fishball Noodles
Unfortunately, the mee pok noodles were a little disappointing. I opted for the spicy version, which had the perfect kick and a good balance of sweet and savoury. Sadly, the noodles were quite alkaline-tasting and the sauce didn’t cling but had a clumpy, gummy texture. On the bright side, it was an extremely generous portion and quite filling.
If I came back, I’d recommend either skipping or getting a small portion of noodles and filling up on more fishballs.
As for the Fishball Noodle Soup with Kway Teow , it features the same amount of handmade fishballs and her giao as the dry version, but with flat, white rice noodles in the soup instead.
Disclaimer: If the fishballs look extra plentiful in this photo, that’s because I combined the noodles with the S $7 Fishball Soup, which comes with more fishballs and her giao than the standard S$ 4 bowl!
As I had them to-go, the noodles had soaked up the soup by the time I got home and became quite soft, easily breaking apart when I held them up with chopsticks. Texturally, it wasn’t too bad and was able to retain some chew despite the long journey home.

I can imagine Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee being best for handmade fishball purists who appreciate labour-intensive ikan parang fishballs. When we stepped into JING , tucked away in a cosy corner of KINEX , I was pleasantly surprised. This buffet restaurant might look unassuming from the outside, but once you step in, you’re greeted by a welcoming atmosphere, friendly staff, and a space decorated with traditional touches.
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
The vibes here are luxurious yet casual. And the menu? Distinctively local and halal-sourced . I don’t visit Muslim-friendly hotpot restaurants that often, so I wasn’t exactly sure what to expect. But let’s just say that after having lunch here, I’m definitely coming back if I get the chance!
The Kopitiam Classics
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
The concept at JING Halal Hotpot & Grill Buffet is simple: each diner gets their own individual hotpot , while every table has a shared grill . Buffet lunch prices for adults start at S$41.90++ on weekdays and from S$47.90++ on weekends . All-you-can-eat dinner prices start at S$47.9++ .
During our weekday lunch at JING, we tried signature menu items themed around ‘ Kopitiam Classics ’ On The Grill , such as Housemade Otah , Hainanese Chicken , and Salted Egg Prawns . My personal recommendation would be the Salted Egg Prawns, which had freshness and flavour that kept me going back for seconds.
Hotpot Broths
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
We also opted for hotpot broths with strong local inspiration – Laksa and Prawn Mee . These flavours might be too rich and savoury for some, but I never felt it was too much for me. I especially loved the Prawn Mee broth, which worked really well with the hotpot ingredients, adding umami goodness to every bite and sip.
Range of Ingredients
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
Speaking of hotpot ingredients, there is quite a wide range to choose from here, especially for meat lovers. Marinated House Specialities include Goji Berry Chicken , Sarawak Black Pepper Beef , Beef Mala , Tom Yum Chicken , and more.
Seafood such as Tiger Prawns , Freshwater Patin Fish , and Black Mussels are also available. Cook your ingredients in your soup of choice or throw them on the grill – it’s up to you how you want to enjoy your meal.
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
There are also ready-to-eat items at one of the counters. Do yourself a favour and get some of these fried mantou with chilli crab sauce . There’s nothing better to have while waiting for your other ingredients to finish cooking.
Desserts
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
Another honourable mention under The Kopitiam Classics menu is the Bubur Pulut Hitam . Yes, desserts are available! And we devoured a bowl of these so quickly. The warm black glutinous rice and coconut cream combination has just the right sweetness and texture that leaves you wanting more.
The Lucky Roll
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
If the food at JING hasn’t convinced you to visit yet, this probably will. From now to 30 December 2026 , groups of 3–6 pax can participate in The Lucky Roll and stand a chance to win an entire meal on the restaurant’s tab.
A S$10 return voucher for 2 is a guaranteed Consolation Prize for eligible groups that participate. The Lucky Roll is only available from Monday to Thursday , 12pm–5pm , so make your reservations with this in mind!
For more information on JING’s menu and bookings, visit their website .
JING Halal Hot Pot & Grill Buffet
Facebook | Instagram | Website
11 Tanjong Katong Road, KINEX Mall, #02-19/20, Singapore 437157
12pm–10pm (Daily)

OGOG: GO is a new Korean cai fan stall at Bugis Junction
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
Believe it or not, I could eat cai fan every day. It’s my go-to option for a fuss-free, affordable, and yummy meal, with countless combinations to choose from. Recently, however, there’s been a surge in Korean-inspired cai png, with eateries putting a modern twist on one of the nation’s most beloved foods. OGOG: GO , a new takeaway kiosk at Bugis Junction , is one of them.
ICYMI: OGOG first debuted last year as a sit-down store at Marina One , serving homestyle Korean food with a cai fan-inspired concept, alongside gimbap and other Korean dishes. They’ve since opened four other outlets in the CBD, catering to busy lunch crowds. Enter OGOG: GO, the brand’s most recent express version of the OG dine-in concept.
Build Your Own Korean Cai Png From $9.90 At This Raffles Place Kiosk
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
The new grab-and-go outlet is located at Basement 1 of Bugis Junction, giving office-goers around the area yet another spot to dabao lunch from. There are 13 dishes to choose from, with prices starting from $8.90 , making it slightly more affordable than their sister brand.
Image credit: Veronica Lumy via Google Maps
Building a bowl here is simple, with a bowl typically comprising one base, one main, and two sides, much like a standard plate of cai fan. Start by picking your desired base. Popular picks include 18-Grain Rice , though there’s also Tofu Noodle or White Rice for something simpler.
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
Moving on to the proteins or mains. Four flavours of chicken are up for grabs, including Signature Soy , as well as Gochujang Dakgalbi and Buldak Cream for a spicy kick. The must-try here would be the Beef Bulgogi for an additional $1 . They also have Soybean Tofu for a vegetarian option.
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
Last but not least, complete your bowl with their selection of sides, featuring classic banchan such as Honey-Glazed Sweet Potatoes , Silky Steamed Egg , and Japchae . For something more unique, they also have Gochujang Broccoli and Perilla Long Beans .
That’s not all—each bowl also comes with your pick of Napa Cabbage Kimchi or Omija Pickled Radish . You also get to top your bowl off with either Gochujang Salsa or Creamy Sesame sauce.
Image credit: OGOG: GO Bugis Junction via Google Maps
If all that food isn’t enough, you can top up $3 to make your bowl a meal, which comes with a soup and a drink. For protein maxxers, add on the Oven-Baked Chicken Bites (from $4.90) , available a la carte in three sizes and two flavours: Classic Gochujang and Soy Garlic .
For more good Korean food, check out our Hanbroth coverage for Busan-style pork soup by a MasterChef Singapore Season 2 winner, or our BB.Q Chicken feature for more deets on the famous Korean fried chicken chain’s opening in Singapore.
Address: 200 Victoria Street, #B1-K06, Bugis Junction, Singapore 188201
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 9pm
Tel: 8227 8068
Website | Full list of outlets
OGOG: GO is not halal-certified.

Foca Kumpir has Turkish baked potatoes in Siglap
Image credit: Foca Kumpir
Singapore’s food scene just got a little more diverse with the opening of Foca Kumpir , the country’s first dedicated Turkish kumpir kiosk. If you’ve never heard of kumpir, it is a popular Turkish street food that’s basically a giant stuffed baked potato.
Image credit: E P via Google Maps
FYI: The new kiosk is helmed by Turkish owner-chef Caner, who named the eatery after Foça, a coastal town near İzmir in his home country.
Unlike the usual baked potatoes we’re familiar with, kumpir is made by mashing the potato with shredded cheese and butter until it turns smooth and fluffy. It’s then loaded with toppings such as olives, gherkins, beef sausages and more.
Image credit: Amon Ho via Google Maps
They have three set options: Plain ($6) , which features just the plain potato base; Classic ($9) ; and Ultimate ($12) , both of which offer three toppings.
Alternatively, you can build your own kumpir, with prices depending on the toppings you pick.
Image credit: EA via Google Maps
Classic toppings ($2 each) include sauteed mushrooms, corn, black olives, and pickled jalapenos. For something more traditional, try the ezme, a Turkish relish made with chopped tomatoes, or atom, a spicy yoghurt dip topped with fried chilli.
Ultimate toppings ($3) include bolognese sauce, shredded chicken, cocktail sausage, and tuna.
Image credit: Sss via Google Maps
Beyond the giant spuds, Foca Kumpir also offers pasta such as Spicy Mushroom Pasta ($11.90) , Tomato Spaghetti ($11.90) , Alfredo Penne ($11.90) and more. If you need a protein boost, you can even add a grilled chicken breast for $5.
Image credit: Foca Kumpir
The dessert offerings are also worth looking at, with unique items such as Olive Oil Chocolate Cake ($6) and Yoghurt Cheesecake ($7) .
Of course, a meal is not complete without a refreshing beverage, and Foca Kumpir offers a range of lemonades, including Classic, Mixed Berry, Peach, Pink Rose , and Tropical ($5 each).
If you’re feeling adventurous, the Ayran ($4) is a savoury yoghurt-based beverage that’s not commonly found in Singapore and is worth a try.
If you’re on the hunt for more Middle Eastern fare and other unique cuisines, check out our Nomad Kitchen review , featuring lesser-seen dishes from seven countries. And while you’re in the area, check out this 12-hour Katong and Joo Chiat itinerary for viral cafes, vintage shopping and more.
Address: 55 Siglap Road, #01-12 Siglap Centre, Singapore 455871
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 9pm
Tel: 8711 2301
Website
Foca Kumpir is not halal-certified but uses no pork or lard.

The Kiri x Monchhichi collaboration is landing in Singapore, pairing bite-sized Kiri Cheesecake Cubes with collectible Monchhichi stickers. It runs from 4 November to 31 December 2026, so there is still time to collect both sets.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
How to get the Kiri x Monchhichi stickers
The mechanic is simple. Buy any two Kiri Cheesecake Cubes or The Laughing Cow Cheez Dipper Solo at participating 7-Eleven stores, and you can redeem one free Kiri x Monchhichi sticker set. There are two sets to collect, handed out at random, so each redemption is a small surprise. Stocks are limited.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
Stickers made for phones, laptops and water bottles
The sticker designs take their cues from the three cheesecake flavours, blending Kiri’s colourful look with Monchhichi’s nostalgic charm. They are meant to be stuck on everyday items such as laptops, notebooks, phone cases and water bottles.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
What are Kiri Cheesecake Cubes?
Kiri Cheesecake Cubes are soft, individually wrapped cheesecake bites inspired by well-loved desserts. The flavours are Strawberry Fraisier, Raspberry Tart and Lemon Tart, and they can be eaten straight from the pack.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
For a little more effort, the brand suggests topping a cube on a biscuit for a quick “1 Second Cheesecake”, or freezing it for a DIY ice cream pop.
Image: Kiri / Bel Group
Our take
It is an easy snack-plus-collectible offer, and the 7-Eleven redemption keeps it convenient. If you like cheese-themed Monchhichi goodies, see our earlier piece on the Laughing Cow x Monchhichi keychains , and for more convenience-store treats, check our 7-Eleven ice cream deals roundup .
Images: Kiri / Bel Group.

deals.body:
New cafes in Singapore with good food for 2026
New aesthetic cafes open in Singapore almost every week, but not all are worth a trip beyond the Instagram photo. This year, we’ve been looking for the ones that put the food first, whether it’s a proper brunch, a standout pastry, or a dessert you’ll want to order again. Here are 10 new cafes in Singapore that opened in 2026 , all serving good food that’s actually worth coming back for.
21 Beautiful Cafes In Singapore For Korean Cube Croissants, Matcha Desserts And More
1. Shared Table
Tucked inside Ang Mo Kio-Bishan Park is Shared Table , a gorgeous garden cafe with nourishing brunch plates. The cafe opened in mid-September 2026 to much fanfare, as it’s also run by the owner of Average Service in Jalan Besar.
The star dish is the Nourish Plate (from $21.90++) , which gets you one grain bowl, one protein, two sides, and a soup of the day. Healthy food sometimes has a reputation for being bland, but that isn’t true here—the Honey Glazed Goji Smoked Duck comes highly recommended with its sweet-savoury glaze, and the Honey Miso Salmon features a house-made honey and miso blend.
Their sides aren’t an afterthought either—our favourites are the Hummus with Roasted Mushroom ($18.90++) and Chicken Skewers ($14.90++) , served with tzatziki and warm pita.
Read our Shared Table review .
Address: Ang Mo Kio-Bishan Park, 1382 Ang Mo Kio Ave 1, Singapore 569932
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 10pm
Website
Shared Table is not halal-certified.
Average Service Founder Opens Garden Cafe In Bishan-AMK Park—Here’s Our Review
2. Noci Bakehouse
After the queues at their Suntec City flagship, Noci Bakehouse built on that buzz with a second outlet at Orchard Gateway . In place of shio pan, the Orchard outlet focuses on Korean bagels, available in 13 sweet and savoury flavours, alongside a small selection of house-made cream cheeses.
Image credit: @nocibakehouse
An outlet-exclusive is the wood-fired panuozzo, an Italian sandwich bread made to order. On our visit, we had the Bulgogi Panuozzo ($18) and Burrata Jambon Panuozzo ($23) , which stacks ham with a whole ball of burrata on top.
Read our Noci Bakehouse feature .
Address: 277 Orchard Road, #01-09/09A, Orchard Gateway, Singapore 238858
Opening hours: Daily 8:30am to 8:30pm
Website
Noci Bakehouse is not halal-certified.
Popular Korean Bakery Opens In Somerset With Wood-Fired Italian Sandwiches
3. Elijah Pies
Image credit: Elijah Pies
Elijah Pies ’ third and largest outlet is a 60-seat flagship that opened in September 2026, taking over a 96-year-old heritage shophouse in Joo Chiat . Fans of the cafe have to order their newly launched Pizza Pies , which are six-inch pies meant for sharing. These decadent pastries are made using laminated dough with 27 layers of French butter, and are baked over a three-day process.
Image credit: Elijah Pies
Flavours include Garlic Ebi ($22++) , Truffle Croque ($24++) , Cheeseburger ($23++) , and Ruffles ($23++) , which is inspired by sour cream and onion chips. For dessert, the Kaya Toffee Pie ($9++) has housemade pandan coconut jam over a hidden layer of gula melaka toffee, while the Souffle Pie ($18++) features chocolate souffle with a warm gianduja centre.
Read our Elijah Pies Joo Chiat feature .
Address: 72 Joo Chiat Place, Singapore 427789
Opening hours: Daily 10am to 10pm
Website
Elijah Pies is not halal-certified.
Elijah Pies Opens Third Cafe In A Joo Chiat Shophouse With Outlet-Exclusive Kaya Pie
4. FreakyNoods Pasta
If you’re a die-hard ice cream and waffle fan, you’ve probably heard of FreakyCones , a popular cafe in Chinatown with an impressive 4.9-star Google rating from over 1K reviews. In July 2026, they launched FreakyNoods Pasta , a new pasta concept on the second floor of their shophouse cafe!
Image credit: FreakyNoods
You can look forward to a small selection of affordable pasta mains here, all priced under $20+ and served in generous portions. Our favourites include Prawn Hub ($16.90+) , an aglio olio dish topped with torched whole prawns, and Beef Daddy ($15.90+) , a Japanese-inspired bolognese featuring a rich, umami-packed beef sauce elevated with garlic confit butter. Don’t miss out on the coffee, either; they serve a mean White ($6+) that’s silky and robust.
Read our FreakyCones feature .
Address: 200 South Bridge Road, Singapore 058749
Pasta hours: Daily 12pm to 3pm, 6pm to 10pm
Website
FreakyNoods is not halal-certified.
FreakyCones: Popular Ice Cream Cafe In Chinatown With 4.9-Star Google Rating
5. Marymount Bakehouse
Image credit: Marymount Bakehouse
What started as a home-based business in 2020 has become one of the more talked-about sourdough bakery-cafes, and Marymount Bakehouse ’s second outlet, after Farrer Park, is now open in Upper Thomson .
…
